As part of that consultation process, the outcome of a data protection impact assessment carried out with regard to the processing at issue may be submitted to the supervisory authority, in particular the measures envisaged to mitigate the risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons.

title: Recital 95
text: The processor should assist the controller, where necessary and upon request, in ensuring compliance with the obligations deriving from the carrying out of data protection impact assessments and from prior consultation of the supervisory authority.

title: Recital 96
text: A consultation of the supervisory authority should also take place in the course of the preparation of a legislative or regulatory measure which provides for the processing of personal data, in order to ensure compliance of the intended processing with this Regulation and in particular to mitigate the risk involved for the data subject.

title: Recital 97
text: Where the processing is carried out by a public authority, except for courts or independent judicial authorities when acting in their judicial capacity, where, in the private sector, processing is carried out by a controller whose core activities consist of processing operations that require regular and systematic monitoring of the data subjects on a large scale, or where the core activities of the controller or the processor consist of processing on a large scale of special categories of personal data and data relating to criminal convictions and offences, a person with expert knowledge of data protection law and practices should assist the controller or processor to monitor internal compliance with this Regulation. In the private sector, the core activities of a controller relate to its primary activities and do not relate to the processing of personal data as ancillary activities. The necessary level of expert knowledge should be determined in particular according to the data processing operations carried out and the protection required for the personal data processed by the controller or the processor. Such data protection officers, whether or not they are an employee of the controller, should be in a position to perform their duties and tasks in an independent manner.

title: Recital 98
text: Associations or other bodies representing categories of controllers or processors should be encouraged to draw up codes of conduct, within the limits of this Regulation, so as to facilitate the effective application of this Regulation, taking account of the specific characteristics of the processing carried out in certain sectors and the specific needs of micro, small and medium enterprises. In particular, such codes of conduct could calibrate the obligations of controllers and processors, taking into account the risk likely to result from the processing for the rights and freedoms of natural persons.

title: Recital 99
text: When drawing up a code of conduct, or when amending or extending such a code, associations and other bodies representing categories of controllers or processors should consult relevant stakeholders, including data subjects where feasible, and have regard to submissions received and views expressed in response to such consultations.

title: Pre-selection of job applications with a language model
text:
Use case: Pre-selection of job applications with a language model

Scenario: A mechanical engineering company with 400 employees receives 150 to 300 applications for every advertised position. The HR department has a language model — an AI system that reads texts and generates texts — read every application and rate on a scale of 1 to 10 how well it matches the job description. Anyone who scores below 6 is not looked at any further. The model is a purchased service accessed through an application programming interface.

Role: Deployer

Classification: High risk (Annex III)

Rationale: Annex III, point 4(a) of the AI Act expressly lists AI systems intended to be used for the recruitment or selection of natural persons, and in doing so names the analysing and filtering of job applications and the evaluation of candidates. That is exactly what the system does. The derogation under Article 6(3) does not apply: the system does not perform a narrow procedural task but materially influences the outcome of decision-making, because a score below 6 removes the application from the procedure.

To do: Use the system only as the provider's instructions for use provide, and actually read the instructions beforehand.; Assign human oversight to a named person who has the necessary competence and the authority to overrule the result.; Inform the works council and affected employees before putting the system into service that it is being used.; Inform applicants that a high-risk AI system takes part in decisions about them.; Check whether the rejection is ultimately borne by a human; a mere rubber-stamp signature is not enough for this.; Ensure sufficient training for the staff who work with the system.; Base the processing of applicants' data on a legal basis and inform applicants in accordance with data protection law.

What matters: Anyone who merely buys and uses an AI system is a deployer and not a provider — but being a deployer is no relief; it is a catalogue of obligations of its own. What determines the classification is not how advanced the technology is, but what purpose the system serves in the procedure. A number that decides who is looked at at all is a selection decision, even if a human formally signs at the end. This question — does the result materially influence the decision? — can be applied to almost any case of your own.

Common mistake: The most common mistake is assuming the use is harmless because "a human decides in the end anyway". If the human only confirms the system's pre-selection and never gets to see the filtered-out applications, human oversight exists only on paper.

title: Mood measurement of customer service employees
text:
Use case: Mood measurement of customer service employees

Scenario: A customer service centre wants to monitor the strain on its employees. An AI system listens in on the telephone calls and infers the employee's emotional state from pitch of voice, speaking rate and pauses: calm, irritated, exhausted. The team leaders receive a daily overview and are to approach employees whose mood stands out. The works council has agreed, and the employees have given their consent.

Role: Deployer

Classification: Prohibited practice

Rationale: Under Article 5(1)(f), the placing on the market, the putting into service and the use of AI systems to infer emotions of a natural person in the workplace are prohibited. The only exception is use for medical or safety reasons — for example fatigue detection for a pilot. Caring about the strain on employees is neither a medical reason in this sense nor a safety reason. Agreement of the works council and consent of the employees change nothing: the prohibition is not at the disposal of the parties involved.

To do: Do not implement the project; an ongoing use must be stopped.; Delete emotion data already collected.; If strain is to be measured, switch to means without emotion inference, such as anonymous surveys or evaluation of the workload.; Check procurement documents for whether purchased systems include emotion features.

What matters: A prohibition knows no compensating measures. With high risk the question is "What do I have to do for it?", with a prohibition "How do I reach the goal differently?". Consent, a works agreement and good intentions do not hold, because here the Regulation prohibits the practice itself. For the workplace and education institutions, emotion inference is the most important of these limits, because it is supplied as an add-on feature in many products.

Common mistake: In the offer, the feature is not called emotion recognition but strain indicator, conversation quality or mood barometer. Anyone who searches only for the word does not find what is prohibited — what matters is whether a person's emotional state is inferred from their characteristics.

title: The information chatbot becomes a pre-selection tool
text:
Use case: The information chatbot becomes a pre-selection tool

Scenario: A temporary employment agency has been running a chatbot on its website for two years that answers prospective candidates' questions about open positions. Now it extends it: in the conversation, the bot asks applicants technical questions and at the end gives the HR department an assessment of whether the applicant appears suitable.

Role: Provider and Deployer

Classification: High risk (Annex III)

Rationale: With the extension, the bot evaluates applicants and thus falls under Annex III, point 4(a). At the same time, Article 25(1)(c) applies: anyone who modifies the intended purpose of a system not classified as high-risk in such a way that it becomes a high-risk AI system is considered a provider. The agency is therefore the provider of the modified system and at the same time its deployer. The transparency obligation under Article 50(1) continues to apply alongside, because the bot talks directly with people.

To do: Treat the change of purpose as a change of role and take on the provider obligations.; Before launching the new function, put the system through the conformity assessment procedure and register it.; Tell applicants that they are talking to an AI system and that it takes part in the selection.; Set up human oversight with the authority to override the assessment.; Check the assessments for discrimination, because conversational behaviour depends heavily on language and origin.

What matters: A change of purpose can turn the user of a system into its provider — precisely when the change lifts the system into high risk. In practice this means: the most dangerous change is the small extension to a long-running, unsuspicious system, because nobody treats it as a new introduction. Anyone who approves changes to AI systems in use without re-classification accumulates exactly these cases.

Common mistake: The extension goes through normal approval as an improvement to the existing bot. Nobody re-checks the classification, and the provider obligations arise without anyone noticing.

title: Cloned voice in the telephone announcement
text:
Use case: Cloned voice in the telephone announcement

Scenario: A car dealership has its telephone announcements generated with the cloned voice of its service manager, so that callers hear a familiar voice. The announcements give opening hours and transfer calls. For new texts the service manager no longer has to record anything; the AI system generates them from written text.

Role: Deployer

Classification: Transparency obligation

Rationale: The announcement generated with a real, recognisable voice is a deep fake within the meaning of the Regulation, because it falsely presents an audio contribution the person did not speak. Under Article 50(4), the deployer must disclose that the content has been artificially generated. In addition, the marking obligation under Article 50(2) applies to the provider of the generating system. The service manager's consent is important for personality rights, but does not replace disclosure to the callers.

To do: Disclose in the announcement that the voice is artificially generated.; Obtain the service manager's written consent to the use of his voice.; Lay down who may approve texts, and restrict access to the voice model.; Settle what happens to the voice model if the service manager leaves the company.

What matters: The consent of the person depicted and disclosure to the audience are two different things with two different addressees. Whoever has the consent may use the voice; whoever uses it must still tell the listener that it is artificial. This applies wherever real people are replicated — and a voice model is an asset that must be managed like an access key, not like an audio file.

Common mistake: The company considers disclosure superfluous because the voice belongs to its own employee and he has agreed. The obligation exists towards the callers and does not depend on the person's consent.

title: Code completion in software development
text:
Use case: Code completion in software development

Scenario: A software house provides its developers with an AI system that suggests the next section of program code while they program. The developers adopt, change or discard the suggestions. The system evaluates no people and generates no outputs for customers.

Role: Deployer

Classification: Minimal risk

Rationale: The system falls into no area of Annex III and touches no prohibited practice. The marking obligation under Article 50(2) targets synthetic audio, image, video or text content that is put into circulation as content; generated program code in an internal development tool is not affected by it. This leaves the AI literacy obligation under Article 4.

To do: Ensure AI literacy of the developers.; Lay down which program code and which access credentials may be entered into the system.; Observe the licensing situation of the suggested program code.; Check the classification of the result if a high-risk AI system is built with the tool — the provider obligations then apply there.

What matters: The tool and the product built with it are classified separately. Code completion is uncritical, even if a high-risk AI system is programmed with it; the obligations then attach to the system built, not to the tool. This separation helps with many development and office tools: you do not have to classify them, but rather what ultimately goes into operation.

Common mistake: Customer data or access keys from test files end up in the inputs. That is not a classification problem, but a data protection and confidentiality problem — and the most common real harm with these tools.

title: Credit scoring for an instalment loan
text:
Use case: Credit scoring for an instalment loan

Scenario: A regional bank checks applications for instalment loans of up to 25000 euros with an AI system. From account transactions, length of employment and credit agency data it calculates a value that estimates the probability of repayment. Below a set value the bank rejects, above it the bank approves; only in the middle range does a clerk look at the application.

Role: Deployer

Classification: High risk (Annex III)

Rationale: Annex III, point 5(b) lists AI systems intended to be used to evaluate the creditworthiness of natural persons or establish their credit score. The system does exactly that. A special feature is added: under Article 27, deployers of systems referred to in Annex III, point 5(b) must carry out a fundamental rights impact assessment before putting the system into use — so here this obligation also applies to a private company, not only to public authorities.

To do: Prepare and keep a fundamental rights impact assessment before putting the system into use.; Inform applicants that a high-risk AI system takes part in the decision.; For the cases in which the system rejects on its own, set up a route for review by a human.; Enable applicants to state their point of view and to contest the decision.; Consider a data protection impact assessment.; Pay attention to the accuracy and suitability of the input data and monitor the system on an ongoing basis.

What matters: The fundamental rights impact assessment under Article 27 does not apply only to public authorities. It applies in addition to two private fields the legislator had particularly in mind: credit scoring, and risk assessment and pricing in life and health insurance. Anyone working in one of these two fields must know this obligation — it is often overlooked because it does not stand out in the general overview of deployer obligations.

Common mistake: Fully automated rejection below the threshold is, in addition, an automated individual decision within the meaning of data protection law and needs its own basis for that, including the right to obtain human intervention. Anyone who checks only the AI Act overlooks this second hurdle.

title: Chatbot on the customer service website
text:
Use case: Chatbot on the customer service website

Scenario: A mail-order retailer puts a chatbot on its website — an AI system that talks with customers in writing. It answers questions about delivery times and returns, looks up orders and hands conversations over to a member of staff when it gets stuck. The bot has a first name and writes in the first person.

Role: Deployer

Classification: Transparency obligation

Rationale: The chatbot falls into no area of Annex III and is therefore not a high-risk AI system. Article 50(1) does apply, however: systems intended to interact directly with natural persons must be designed so that the persons are informed that they are interacting with an AI system — unless this is obvious from the circumstances. A bot with a human first name that writes in the first person is precisely not making it obvious.

To do: At the start of every conversation, make clear that an AI system is answering here, not a member of staff.; Place the notice where it is read, not only in the terms of use.; Offer a way to reach a human and also name it.; Ensure AI literacy of the employees who look after the bot.; Re-check the classification if the bot is to make decisions about customers.

What matters: The transparency obligation under Article 50 is a separate drawer next to the risk classification. A system can be completely uncritical and still trigger an obligation, simply because people talk to it or it generates content. Anyone who only looks for high risk regularly overlooks these obligations — and in practice they affect far more companies than the high-risk rules, because almost every business uses a bot or a text tool somewhere.

Common mistake: The notice is in the terms of use or disappears after the first message. It is then not obvious, and that is exactly what the provision requires.

title: General trust score for customers
text:
Use case: General trust score for customers

Scenario: An online retailer creates a trust score for every customer. It is derived from payment behaviour, return rate, tone in messages to customer service and reviews the customer has left. The score not only decides on payment in advance but is passed on to a subsidiary that brokers rental flats and does not pass on applicants with a low score to landlords.

Role: Deployer

Classification: Prohibited practice

Rationale: Article 5(1)(c) prohibits the evaluation or classification of natural persons over a certain period of time based on their social behaviour or personal characteristics, where the evaluation leads to detrimental treatment in a context unrelated to the context in which the data were originally generated, or to detrimental treatment that is disproportionate. Both are likely here: tone towards customer service and the return rate from online retail determine access to a flat.

To do: Stop passing the score on to the flat brokerage.; Abandon condensing behavioural characteristics into a general trust score.; Where it is needed, assess the risk of payment default for a specific purpose and separately, instead of as a general assessment of the person.; Check which decisions are already based on the score, and correct them.

What matters: The core of the prohibition does not lie in evaluating, but in transferring into an unrelated context. A risk assessment for one's own, factually connected purpose is not the same as a general score about a person that follows them everywhere. The useful question for your own cases is therefore: where do the data come from, and where do they take effect? The further apart these two points are, the closer you are to the prohibition.

Common mistake: The score is justified as fraud prevention. But the exception for fraud detection in Annex III, point 5 is a rule about the high-risk classification and does not lift the prohibition of social scoring under Article 5.

title: Converting CVs into a uniform data-field format
text:
Use case: Converting CVs into a uniform data-field format

Scenario: A software house offers HR departments a tool that reads submitted CVs from text files and transfers the information into fixed fields: name, qualification, previous employers, periods. It assesses nothing, classifies nothing and sorts nothing. The HR department then reads the applications itself.

Role: Provider

Classification: Exemption under Article 6(3)

Rationale: The use lies in the area of recruitment and selection and thus in Annex III, point 4, so the derogation must be checked. It applies under Article 6(3)(a): converting unstructured information into a fixed format is a narrow procedural task. The system poses no significant risk and does not materially influence the outcome of decision-making, because it forms no statement about the applicants; no profiling takes place. As provider, the software house must document this assessment under Article 6(4) before the system is placed on the market, and register itself and the system in the EU database under Article 49(2).

To do: Document the assessment that the derogation applies before the system is placed on the market.; Register yourself and the system in the EU database.; Provide the assessment to the competent authorities upon request.; Make clear in the product description that the tool does not assess and does not sort.; Carry out the assessment again as soon as a function for classification or ranking is added.

What matters: Anyone relying on the derogation has obligations precisely for that reason: the derogation takes the system out of the heavy requirements, not out of the Regulation. Under Article 6(4) the assessment must be documented before placing on the market, and under Article 49(2) registration is added. The legislator thus deliberately made the derogation a verifiable decision — nobody is to be able to claim it for themselves tacitly.

Common mistake: The software house regards the tool as mere data preparation with no connection to the AI Act and documents and registers nothing. But because the area of use lies in Annex III, exactly this documentation is required.

title: Advertising that targets financial hardship
text:
Use case: Advertising that targets financial hardship

Scenario: A provider of short-term small loans advertises online. An AI system recognises from search behaviour and usage patterns which users are probably in acute financial hardship, and repeatedly shows precisely these users advertisements with urgency messages at night. In doing so, the system learns which approach most often leads to a contract with this group.

Role: Deployer

Classification: Prohibited practice

Rationale: Article 5(1)(b) prohibits AI systems that exploit any of the vulnerabilities of persons due to their age, disability or a specific social or economic situation, with the objective or the effect of materially distorting the behaviour of those persons, in a manner that causes or is reasonably likely to cause significant harm. Economic hardship is such a situation, the targeted delivery exploits it, and further indebtedness is significant harm. That users formally decide freely does not hold — the prohibition applies precisely where freedom of decision is undermined.

To do: Stop delivery based on characteristics of hardship.; No target-group formation that takes economic distress, age or disability as its starting point.; Check whether the design of the advertisements additionally falls under the prohibition of manipulative or deceptive techniques under point (a).; Limit advertising optimisation so that it does not drift on its own towards vulnerability.

What matters: Optimising systems find weaknesses by themselves, even if nobody specified that. Anyone who optimises a system for closing rate may get as a result precisely the approach that people in distress are least able to resist. That is why it is not enough to have no prohibited intention: Article 5(1)(b) covers the objective and the effect. Anyone using such systems must check what they actually drift towards.

Common mistake: The company considers itself uninvolved because it did not describe the target group; the system found it. The effect is sufficient for the prohibition.

title: Commercial with a replicated actor
text:
Use case: Commercial with a replicated actor

Scenario: A brewery shoots a commercial and, for two scenes, has an AI system put the face of a well-known actor onto an extra. The actor agreed to this for a fee. The commercial runs on television and on video platforms.

Role: Deployer

Classification: Transparency obligation

Rationale: A face swap involving a real, recognisable person is a deep fake. Under Article 50(4), the deployer must disclose that the content has been artificially generated or manipulated. For evidently artistic, creative, satirical or fictional works, the obligation is limited to disclosing the existence of such content in an appropriate manner that does not hamper the display or enjoyment of the work. A commercial is not such a work in the usual understanding; whether a recognisably fictional staging falls under it depends on the design and is not decided here.

To do: Disclose in the commercial or in its immediate vicinity that image content has been artificially generated.; Put the actor's consent in writing and limit the scope of use in it.; Ensure machine-readable marking with the generating service.; Record which scenes were edited, so that the disclosure can be evidenced.

What matters: The exception for artistic works relaxes disclosure; it does not lift it: disclosing the existence of generated content in an appropriate manner is still required. Anyone wanting to rely on it therefore still has to do something, only more discreetly. In advertising, pointing to art is a weak argument anyway, because the purpose of the staging is selling.

Common mistake: The disclosure moves into the end credits or the video description and does not reach the viewer. A disclosure is appropriate only if it appears where the content is perceived.

title: Fine-tuning a purchased language model on in-house technical texts
text:
Use case: Fine-tuning a purchased language model on in-house technical texts

Scenario: An engineering firm takes a freely available language model and fine-tunes it with 12000 of its own inspection reports — that is, it continues training the model with its own texts so that it masters the firm's technical language. The fine-tuned model runs on the firm's own server and helps the engineers draft new reports. The firm passes none of this on to outsiders.

Role: Deployer

Classification: Minimal risk

Rationale: Fine-tuning alone does not make the firm a provider of a general-purpose AI model: it places nothing on the market and puts nothing into service under its own name for others, but uses the model internally. The use touches no area of Annex III and no prohibited practice, so this leaves the AI literacy obligation under Article 4. The classification shifts as soon as the firm makes the model available to third parties or uses it for tasks from Annex III.

To do: Ensure AI literacy of the engineers who work with the model.; Check whether the licence of the base model permits fine-tuning and the use.; Clarify whether the inspection reports contain personal data or third parties' trade secrets.; Record which base model was used, in which version.; Reassess the classification as soon as the model is passed on to outsiders.

What matters: Internal use and placing on the market are the dividing line between deployer and provider obligations. Anyone who fine-tunes a model only for themselves and uses it themselves remains a deployer; anyone who makes it available to others becomes a provider and takes on a considerably heavier catalogue. Companies often cross this line without noticing, for example when an internal tool is passed on to a subsidiary or to customers to make things easier.

Common mistake: The training data are not checked. Inspection reports often contain names of employees and customers, and a model can reproduce such information in its outputs.

title: Emergency braking assistant for commercial vehicles
text:
Use case: Emergency braking assistant for commercial vehicles

Scenario: A supplier develops an emergency braking assistant. An AI system detects obstacles from camera and radar data and automatically triggers full braking. The part is placed on the market as a vehicle component and is subject to vehicle type-approval.

Role: Provider

Classification: High risk (Annex I)

Rationale: The AI system is a safety component of a vehicle. The vehicle rules are among the legislation listed in Annex I, and Article 6(1) classifies such systems as high-risk if the product is required to undergo a third-party assessment. For this route via Annex I, application under Article 113 begins later than for Annex III; the exact current status of the deadlines must be checked with the competent authority before any decision with legal consequences.

To do: Establish risk management throughout the lifecycle, including the cases in which the system triggers wrongly.; Define and measure accuracy and robustness also in poor visibility, wet conditions and dirt.; Provide for cybersecurity, because a manipulated braking system directly endangers people.; Incorporate the requirements into the type-approval procedure.; Record and evaluate incidents in the field.

What matters: Not every piece of software in a vehicle falls into high risk via Annex I — what matters is whether it is a safety component and whether the product legislation requires assessment by a third party. An infotainment system does not meet this; a braking intervention does. For your own cases, the useful question is: what happens if this function fails or triggers wrongly? Anyone who then has to describe a physical danger is very probably looking at a safety component.

Common mistake: The company treats the AI Act as a topic for later, because the deadline for Annex I takes effect later. But the requirements for data and documentation cannot be retrofitted onto a finished model — they determine how development is done.

title: Continuous evaluation of computer use in the office
text:
Use case: Continuous evaluation of computer use in the office

Scenario: A service provider installs software on all office computers that records keyboard activity, application switches and break times. An AI system evaluates the recordings and reports to management every week which employees' activity deviates noticeably from the team average.

Role: Deployer

Classification: High risk (Annex III)

Rationale: Annex III, point 4(b) covers AI systems for monitoring and evaluating the performance and behaviour of workers. Ongoing evaluation with reports to management is exactly that. Independently of the AI Act, whether such continuous monitoring is permissible under data protection law is a separate and very narrow question; whether seamless recording is proportionate depends on purpose and design and is not decided here.

To do: Before anything else, clarify whether monitoring at this depth is permissible under data protection law at all.; Consider a data protection impact assessment — with systematic monitoring of employees it is the obvious step.; Inform the workers' representatives and employees; clarify co-determination rights.; Name a person for human oversight and give employees a way to present their side.

What matters: Two sets of rules apply side by side, and the stricter one decides practice. The AI Act says which obligations apply to the use; it does not permit the use. A system can meet all obligations of the AI Act and still be impermissible under data protection law. The order of the check is therefore: am I allowed to at all? And only then: what must I observe in doing so?

Common mistake: The use is justified with the employees' consent. In an employment relationship, because of the dependency, consent is freely given only under narrow conditions — anyone who cannot refuse without fearing disadvantages does not consent freely.

title: Training suggestions for employees
text:
Use case: Training suggestions for employees

Scenario: An industrial company offers its employees a learning platform on the intranet. An AI system suggests courses to each employee based on their job and the courses they have already attended. The suggestions are non-binding, are not reported to supervisors and play no role in appraisals or promotions.

Role: Deployer

Classification: Minimal risk

Rationale: The recommendation touches none of the cases in Annex III, point 4: it takes no part in recruitment, promotion, termination, contractual terms, allocation of tasks or performance evaluation, because it is shown to the employee alone and has no consequences in the employment relationship. This leaves the AI literacy obligation under Article 4. The classification flips as soon as the suggestions or whether they are taken up feed into appraisals or are reported to management.

To do: Ensure that the people working with the system are sufficiently trained.; Record and observe that suggestions and whether they are taken up do not feed into appraisals.; Inform employees which data the platform uses.

What matters: The same technology at the same place in the company can fall into two risk classes — it depends on who gets to see the result and what happens with it. The route to an uncritical classification here does not lead through weaker technology but through a deliberate boundary in the procedure: the recommendation stays with the employee. Such boundaries are the most effective and cheapest lever a company has — but only if they are binding and observed.

Common mistake: After a year, HR development wants an evaluation of who takes up the suggestions. The result thereby moves into performance assessment and the case is a different one — the boundary falls in passing, without anyone re-checking the classification.

title: Automated grading of free-text answers in an exam
text:
Use case: Automated grading of free-text answers in an exam

Scenario: A vocational academy has the free-text answers of its final exams graded by an AI system. The system awards points per answer and proposes a grade. The examiner sees the proposals and corrects about every tenth paper by sampling; she adopts the remaining grades.

Role: Deployer

Classification: High risk (Annex III)

Rationale: Annex III, point 3(b) lists AI systems intended to be used to evaluate learning outcomes. Awarding grades in a final exam is exactly that. The derogation under Article 6(3) does not apply: the grading is not a narrow procedural task and materially influences the outcome, especially as nine out of ten grades are adopted unchanged.

To do: Inform examinees that a high-risk AI system takes part in the grading.; Design human oversight so that grades can be reviewed reliably, not only by sampling.; Provide a procedure through which examinees can challenge the grading and obtain a review by a human.; Use the system according to the provider's instructions for use and monitor its accuracy on an ongoing basis.; Ensure sufficient training for the examiners in handling the system.

What matters: A sample is a quality check, but not human oversight of the individual decision. Anyone who adopts the grade unseen for nine out of ten papers has made no assessment of their own for those nine. Human oversight within the meaning of the Regulation means that the person exercising oversight can examine the individual case, has the time and access to do so and may change the result — not that they appear somewhere in the procedure.

Common mistake: The institution considers itself safe because the examiner formally awards the grade. But someone who has never read the exam does not award the grade; they pass it on.

title: Rejection of an application without any human involvement
text:
Use case: Rejection of an application without any human involvement

Scenario: A mobile network operator checks applications for a contract with a device fully automatically. An AI system assesses creditworthiness and, at a score below the threshold, rejects immediately; the applicant receives a rejection by email within seconds. No member of staff sees the case.

Role: Deployer

Classification: High risk (Annex III)

Rationale: Under the AI Act this is a high-risk use, because Annex III, point 5(b) covers evaluating creditworthiness and establishing credit scores. Alongside it stands a second, independent hurdle: Article 22 of the General Data Protection Regulation gives the data subject the right not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing which produces legal effects concerning him or her or similarly significantly affects him or her. This is permissible only in the cases named there — for example if it is necessary for entering into a contract or the person has given explicit consent — and then at least the right to obtain human intervention, to express his or her point of view and to contest the decision must be safeguarded.

To do: Check which of the cases named in Article 22 the fully automated decision is based on, and record this.; Set up a procedure through which the applicant can obtain human intervention.; Point out this right in the rejection, not only in the privacy notice.; Provide information about the logic of the decision in an understandable form.; In addition, fulfil the obligations as deployer of the high-risk system, including the fundamental rights impact assessment.

What matters: The two sets of rules ask different questions. The AI Act asks which obligations apply to the use. Data protection law asks whether a decision may be taken fully automatically at all. Anyone who fully meets the obligations of the AI Act has thereby not yet done anything about Article 22. Moreover, human oversight under the AI Act and the right to obtain human intervention under Article 22 are not the same: one is addressed to the business, the other is a right of the data subject that he or she can assert.

Common mistake: The company regards human oversight under the AI Act as fulfilling Article 22. Oversight that the data subject cannot invoke does not replace his or her right to obtain human intervention.

title: Generated product images in the online shop
text:
Use case: Generated product images in the online shop

Scenario: A furniture retailer no longer has its living room furniture photographed, but has an AI system depict it in designed rooms. The images show the sofa in question in a flat that does not exist. The retailer uses a purchased image service for this and puts the results in its shop.

Role: Deployer

Classification: Transparency obligation

Rationale: Generating images triggers transparency obligations. Under Article 50(2), the provider of the generating system must ensure that the outputs are marked in a machine-readable format as artificially generated — this obligation falls on the image service, not on the retailer. Under Article 50(4), the retailer must disclose when it generates or manipulates content that constitutes a deep fake. Depictions of invented rooms with real products are as a rule not deep fakes, because they do not falsely present existing persons, places or events; but as soon as a real place or a recognisable person is shown, the assessment flips. Competition law is independent of this.

To do: Ask the image service and obtain confirmation that the outputs are marked in a machine-readable format.; Do not remove the marking when uploading to the shop — cropping and converting often delete it.; Ensure that the depiction does not make the product look different from what it is.; Check as soon as real places or recognisable persons come into the picture; the disclosure obligation for deep fakes then applies.

What matters: With generated content, the obligations rest on two shoulders: the provider of the tool marks in a machine-readable way, the deployer discloses deep fakes. Anyone buying a tool does not automatically inherit the marking — they must check whether it is present and must not destroy it during further processing. For your own cases, the question is worthwhile: who in my chain is provider, who is deployer, and which of the two obligations therefore falls on me?

Common mistake: The marking sits in the metadata of the image file and is lost when cropping or converting to another format. The retailer thinks it has delivered what the service promised, and deletes the marking itself in the next work step.

title: Checking whether teachers deviate from their grading pattern
text:
Use case: Checking whether teachers deviate from their grading pattern

Scenario: A school authority has an AI system evaluate the grade distribution of past years. It reports when a teacher grades markedly differently in one course than in their other courses. The report goes to the school inspectorate, which then seeks a conversation with the teacher. The system does not change or assess the grades of individual pupils.

Role: Deployer

Classification: Exemption under Article 6(3)

Rationale: The education area is covered by Annex III, point 3, so the derogation must be checked. It applies under Article 6(3)(c): the system detects decision-making patterns and deviations from prior patterns and is not meant to replace or influence the previously completed human assessment without proper human review. The pupils' grades remain untouched. At the same time, the case shows the double-sidedness: towards the teachers, the system is monitoring and evaluation of work performance and can thus fall under Annex III, point 4 — for them, the derogation cannot be taken for granted.

To do: Document the assessment that the derogation applies for the education part.; For the teachers, check separately whether this is performance monitoring of employees, and fulfil the resulting obligations.; Inform the staff council and teachers about the use.; Ensure that a report is only an occasion for a conversation and not itself an evaluation of the teacher.

What matters: A system may need to be checked from two directions at once, because it affects two groups of people. For the pupils it is a pattern check and falls under the derogation; for the teachers it is monitoring of work performance. Anyone who thinks only of the obviously affected persons in a case of their own loses sight of the second group — and it has rights of its own, often even more extensive ones.

Common mistake: The school authority checks only the education area and entirely overlooks the employee dimension. That the teachers must be informed in advance then falls by the wayside too.

title: Risk assessment and premium in private health insurance
text:
Use case: Risk assessment and premium in private health insurance

Scenario: A private health insurer assesses new applications with an AI system. From the answers in the health questionnaire and the age, it estimates the expected benefit costs and uses this to propose a risk surcharge, which application processing adopts or changes after consulting the medical service.

Role: Deployer

Classification: High risk (Annex III)

Rationale: Annex III, point 5(c) lists AI systems intended to be used for risk assessment and pricing in relation to natural persons in the case of life and health insurance. Both apply. As with credit scoring, the obligation to carry out a fundamental rights impact assessment under Article 27 applies here too. That processing can change the proposal does not change the classification, because the system materially influences pricing.

To do: Prepare a fundamental rights impact assessment before putting the system into use.; Inform applicants that the system takes part.; Set up human oversight with a real power to change the result, not just a confirmation box.; For processing the health information, observe the special requirements for health data.; Regularly check the proposals for unlawful discrimination.

What matters: Not every insurance falls under this area: the Annex names life and health insurance, not insurance in general. Motor or household contents insurance is not covered by Annex III, point 5(c). The reason is obvious once you read the purpose of the provision: it is about access to essential services. When reading Annex III it is therefore worth paying attention to every restrictive word — the areas are drawn more narrowly than the headings suggest.

Common mistake: The insurer transfers the assessment unchecked to other lines of insurance and takes on unnecessary obligations there — or, conversely, concludes from the absence of motor insurance in the list that nothing applies in health insurance either.

title: A company trains its own base model and releases it
text:
Use case: A company trains its own base model and releases it

Scenario: A software house trains its own language model from scratch and makes it available to other companies through an application programming interface so that they can build it into their products. The model can be used for many different tasks: writing, summarising, classifying and translating texts.

Role: Provider

Classification: General-purpose AI model

Rationale: A model that can be used for many different tasks is a general-purpose AI model. Whoever makes it available under their own name is its provider and owes the obligations under Article 53. Under Article 51(2), the model is presumed to have systemic risk when the cumulative amount of computation used for its training is greater than 10 to the power of 25 floating-point operations; the presumption is rebuttable, and the Commission can also designate a model without this threshold. If that applies, the obligations under Article 55 are added.

To do: Draw up and keep up to date the technical documentation of the model, including its training and testing process and the results of its evaluation.; Provide the companies that build the model in with information enabling them to comply with their own obligations.; Put in place a policy to comply with copyright law, including observing expressed reservations of rights.; Publish a summary of the content used for training.; Record the amount of computation used for training, so that the threshold for systemic risk can be assessed.; In the case of systemic risk, perform model evaluation including adversarial testing, mitigate risks and report serious incidents.

What matters: Models and systems are two different things in the Regulation, with two different sets of rules. A general-purpose AI model is not classified under Annex III but has its own obligations in Articles 53 to 55. Anyone who makes such a model available therefore does not need to ask in which area it is used — the obligations apply to them regardless, and the question of use only arises for whoever builds a system from it.

Common mistake: For models released under a free and open-source licence, two of the obligations from Article 53(1) do not apply — but only under the licence conditions stated there and not where there is systemic risk. Anyone relying on open source must observe the conditions exactly.

title: Sorting incoming mail by responsibility
text:
Use case: Sorting incoming mail by responsibility

Scenario: An insurance company has an AI system read the daily incoming mail and sort it by type of letter: claim notification, contract change, complaint, invoice. The system files each letter in the folder of the responsible department. It does not assess how the case will turn out and does not assign urgency.

Role: Deployer

Classification: Exemption under Article 6(3)

Rationale: Because the insurer also provides health and life insurance, the pre-sorting touches an area that may be covered by Annex III, point 5(c). The derogation under Article 6(3) does apply, however: classification by type of letter is a narrow procedural task under point (a) and at the same time a preparatory task under point (d); it does not materially influence the outcome of decision-making, and no profiling takes place. Under Article 6(4), the assessment must be documented.

To do: Document the assessment that the derogation applies before putting the system into use.; Ensure by technical and organisational means that the system assigns no urgency and no prospect of success.; Catch wrongly sorted letters so that no deadlines are missed.; Ensure AI literacy of the staff handling incoming mail.

What matters: A task is preparatory only if the actual assessment really still takes place afterwards. Sorting by type of letter is preparatory; sorting by prospect of success no longer is, because it already sets the direction of the decision. For many document tools, the classification is decided at this boundary — and it is often only one product feature away.

Common mistake: With its next release, the provider supplies an urgency rating that is switched on as a convenience feature. The basis of the derogation thereby falls away without anyone renewing the assessment.

title: Emotion analysis in a video job interview
text:
Use case: Emotion analysis in a video job interview

Scenario: A company conducts first interviews as recorded video interviews. An AI system evaluates facial expressions and voice and gives indications of the applicant's enthusiasm, insecurity and resilience, which feed into the selection alongside the professional assessment.

Role: Deployer

Classification: Prohibited practice

Rationale: Article 5(1)(f) prohibits inferring emotions in the workplace. The application procedure belongs to this area; the provision protects not only employees but the workplace context. The exception for medical or safety reasons does not apply. This means the emotion analysis part is not merely impermissible — it is prohibited, whereas the pre-selection as such would merely be high-risk under Annex III, point 4. Article 50(3) must also be borne in mind, which provides for an information obligation for permitted emotion recognition systems; it does not permit any use that is prohibited under Article 5.

To do: Switch off the emotion analysis; delete the records of the evaluated characteristics.; Treat the remaining professional pre-selection as a high-risk use and fulfil its obligations.; Inform applicants about the use of the remaining system.; In future procurement, have it excluded that evaluations of facial expressions and voice are included.

What matters: A project can consist of several parts that are to be classified differently — and the prohibited part does not make the whole prohibited, but has to come out. After that, the rest remains to be checked, here as a high-risk use. This decomposition is the right way to deal with composite systems: classify not the product but its functions, and then remove the impermissible one instead of defending the whole.

Common mistake: The company relies on Article 50(3) providing an information obligation for emotion recognition, and concludes from this that the use is permissible with information. This provision applies only to uses that are not already prohibited under Article 5.

title: Proposal list for staff reductions
text:
Use case: Proposal list for staff reductions

Scenario: A retail chain has to cut positions in its administration. The HR department has an AI system evaluate the personnel files and generate a list, sorted by criteria, of which employment relationships the system considers easiest to terminate. The list goes into the negotiations with the works council.

Role: Deployer

Classification: High risk (Annex III)

Rationale: Annex III, point 4(b) lists AI systems for making decisions affecting the termination of work-related contractual relationships. That the system does not itself give notice changes nothing: the Regulation starts from influencing the decision, and a proposal list that becomes the basis for negotiations influences it. The derogation under Article 6(3) does not apply, since the system evaluates individual employees and thereby performs profiling.

To do: Set up human oversight so that the list is reviewed and not simply adopted.; Inform the workers' representatives and affected employees about the use.; Record in a traceable way the criteria used for sorting, and check the criteria for unlawful discrimination.; Check whether evaluating the personnel files for this purpose is permissible.

What matters: "The system does not decide, it only proposes" makes no legal difference if the proposal shapes the course of the decision. The Regulation covers taking part in the decision, not only the decision itself. For your own cases, this means: do not ask whether the system takes the last step, but whether its result sets the direction the last step then takes.

Common mistake: Sorting criteria that look neutral can discriminate indirectly — for example when part-time work, parental leave or sick days feed in and certain groups therefore regularly end up at the top of the list.

title: Camera-based quality inspection in manufacturing
text:
Use case: Camera-based quality inspection in manufacturing

Scenario: A supplier inspects stamped sheet-metal parts for cracks and dimensional deviations with a camera and an AI system. Detected parts are ejected, the rest carries on. Parts are inspected, not people; the camera is pointed at the conveyor.

Role: Deployer

Classification: Minimal risk

Rationale: The system assesses workpieces, not people, and falls into no area of Annex III. High risk via Annex I would only be possible if the system were a safety component of a machine whose conformity assessment required a third party — that is not the case for a mere quality inspection downstream of the process. This leaves the AI literacy obligation under Article 4. It would be different if the inspection also evaluated the performance of the operators; Annex III, point 4 would then apply.

To do: Ensure AI literacy of the employees at the installation.; Ensure that the inspection results are not attributed to operators and used for performance evaluation.; Monitor the detection quality, because defects that slip through become a product problem.; Re-check the classification if the system intervenes in the machine control.

What matters: The AI Act classifies by the persons affected, not by technology. The same image recognition is uncritical for sheet-metal parts and high-risk or even prohibited for faces. The first question in any case of your own is therefore not how good or new the model is, but: is something being said here about people? If the answer is no, the check is short.

Common mistake: The ejection rate is evaluated per shift and operator in order to find carelessness. The same system thereby evaluates the behaviour of employees and falls under Annex III, point 4.

title: Software that pre-reads X-ray images
text:
Use case: Software that pre-reads X-ray images

Scenario: A medical technology company develops software that searches chest X-ray images for abnormalities and presents marked areas to the radiologist with an indication of urgency. The software is placed on the market as a medical device and for this requires assessment by an independent body.

Role: Provider

Classification: High risk (Annex I)

Rationale: Under Article 6(1), an AI system is high-risk if it is a safety component of a product covered by Annex I or is itself such a product, and that product is required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment. The medical device rules are listed in Annex I, and assessment by an independent body is required here. The classification therefore does not run through Annex III but through product safety law — a separate route with its own date of application, which under Article 113 begins later than the one for Annex III.

To do: Establish and maintain a risk management system throughout the entire lifecycle.; Check the training, validation and testing data for suitability, completeness and biases, and document this.; Draw up the technical documentation and keep it up to date.; Build human oversight into the design from the outset: the radiologist must be able to override markings.; Define, measure and declare accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity.; Combine the conformity assessment with the medical device assessment instead of running two separate procedures.

What matters: There are two mutually independent routes into high risk: via Annex III according to the area of use, and via Annex I according to the product in which the AI is embedded. Anyone who reads only Annex III does not find medical devices, machinery or vehicles there and wrongly concludes that the risk is low. For manufacturers, the good news is that the AI Act builds on the existing product assessments: the requirements belong in the existing procedure, not alongside it.

Common mistake: The company runs the requirements of the AI Act as a second, separate procedure alongside the medical device assessment — double work and contradictory documentation are the result.

title: Scheduling suggestions for meetings
text:
Use case: Scheduling suggestions for meetings

Scenario: A consultancy uses an AI system that suggests free time slots for meetings from the participants' calendars. It takes into account working hours, travel times and the length of the meeting. Who is invited is decided by the person sending the invitation.

Role: Deployer

Classification: Minimal risk

Rationale: The system sorts time slots, not people. It takes no part in recruitment, promotion, termination, contractual terms, allocation of tasks or performance evaluation and therefore does not fall under Annex III, point 4. No other area of Annex III applies either. This leaves the AI literacy obligation under Article 4. A derogation check under Article 6(3) is not needed, because Annex III is not even engaged.

To do: Ensure AI literacy of the employees.; Do not evaluate the calendar data for other purposes, for example for attendance control.

What matters: The check follows a fixed order, and it should not be skipped: first prohibited practice, then Annex I, then Annex III, then the derogation, then transparency. Anyone who never reaches Annex III does not need to think about Article 6(3) — the derogation exists only for systems that would otherwise be high-risk. In practice this distinction saves a great deal of work, because by far most workplace tools drop out already at the question of the area.

Common mistake: Scheduling turns into an evaluation of who has missed how many meetings. The system thereby moves into monitoring the behaviour of employees and falls under Annex III, point 4.

title: Data processing agreement with the model provider
text:
Use case: Data processing agreement with the model provider

Scenario: A tax advisory firm wants to use a language model that summarises client letters. The model provider makes a standard data processing agreement available. In it, the provider reserves the right to use inputs to improve its services and to engage sub-processors listed on its website.

Role: Deployer

Classification: Minimal risk

Rationale: Summarising letters falls into no area of Annex III; this leaves the AI literacy obligation under Article 4. The question under data protection law is the allocation of roles: a processor may use data only on the instructions of the controller. A reservation to use inputs for its own purposes does not fit with this — to that extent the provider acts for its own purposes and is itself a controller in that respect. For tax advisers, the professional duty of confidentiality is added, which imposes its own requirements on involving third parties.

To do: Have the reservation to use the inputs for own purposes contractually excluded, or switch provider.; Check the list of sub-processors and agree a right to object to changes.; Check whether the professional duty of confidentiality permits involving this provider.; Lay down technical and organisational measures specifically in the contract, not just name them in general terms.; Lay down which client data may be entered into the system at all, and tell the staff so in binding terms.

What matters: A standard data processing agreement is no proof that everything is in order — it is an offer that you read. The decisive passage is always the same: may the provider also use the inputs for itself? If it says yes, there is to that extent no processing on instructions, and the agreement does not support the project. For persons bound by professional secrecy, a further barrier is added that is independent of data protection law.

Common mistake: The agreement is signed because it exists and has been provided by the provider. Nobody reads the clause on use of the inputs, and it is precisely that clause that decides whether the use is permissible.

title: Preliminary review of applications in a municipal authority
text:
Use case: Preliminary review of applications in a municipal authority

Scenario: A city administration pre-checks applications for a municipal assistance benefit with an AI system. It reads the submitted documents, compares the information with the eligibility requirements and flags applications where, in its view, the requirements are not met. Case handlers process the flagged applications first and mostly reject them.

Role: Deployer

Classification: High risk (Annex III)

Rationale: Annex III, point 5(a) covers AI systems intended to be used by public authorities or on their behalf to evaluate the eligibility of natural persons for essential public assistance benefits and services, and to grant, reduce, revoke or reclaim such benefits and services. The flagging is such an evaluation. That it formally only pre-sorts does not hold, because in practice the flagging predetermines the rejection. As a public authority, the city is also subject to the obligation to carry out a fundamental rights impact assessment under Article 27.

To do: Carry out a fundamental rights impact assessment before putting the system into use.; Inform applicants that the system takes part.; Ensure that flagged applications are examined fully on their merits and not just rejected faster.; Evaluate how often case handlers disagree with the flagging — if this number stays at zero, oversight is only formal.; Give reasons for rejections in a way that allows the applicant to contest them.

What matters: A pre-sorting that is always followed in practice is a decision. Whether human oversight works can be measured: how often does the human deviate from the proposal? This number is the best self-test a deployer has, and it can be applied to any case of your own. If it stays at zero over time, it is not that the technology is especially good, but that oversight is not there.

Common mistake: The authority relies on the derogation under Article 6(3) for a preparatory task. A task is preparatory only if the assessment really still takes place afterwards — a flagging that determines the rejection is not preparation.

title: Fraud detection in payment transactions
text:
Use case: Fraud detection in payment transactions

Scenario: The same regional bank has a second AI system check all card payments in real time. If it detects a pattern indicating a misused card, it holds the payment and reports it to the fraud department, which calls the customer. The value plays no role in lending and is not stored there either.

Role: Deployer

Classification: Exemption under Article 6(3)

Rationale: Annex III, point 5(b) expressly excludes from the high-risk classification AI systems used for the purpose of detecting financial fraud. This exception is in the legal text itself and is not the general derogation under Article 6(3); it applies as long as the purpose really is fraud detection. What matters is clean separation: as soon as the value feeds into credit scoring, the purpose is no longer just fraud detection and the exception no longer holds.

To do: Lay down fraud detection as the purpose and ensure technically that the value does not reach the credit decision.; Document why the exception is relied on.; Ensure AI literacy of the employees working with it.; Provide prompt clarification by humans for held payments.; Check under data protection law whether holding a payment is to be treated as an automated individual decision.

What matters: There are two different kinds of exceptions, and they are often confused. One is in the Annex itself and takes a purpose out of the area — here, fraud detection. The other is Article 6(3) and applies only if the system does not materially influence the decision. The first goes further but demands purpose discipline: it falls as soon as the result is used for something else. Purpose limitation is not a formality here but the very reason the exception exists.

Common mistake: The fraud value is stored in the data pool and later moves into the credit check as a handy additional feature. This creates, after the fact, a high-risk use that nobody decided on.

title: Predictive maintenance for the company's own machinery
text:
Use case: Predictive maintenance for the company's own machinery

Scenario: A paper manufacturer evaluates the vibration and temperature data of its pumps and rollers with an AI system. It predicts which bearing is likely to show abnormalities in the coming weeks and generates maintenance orders for the maintenance department from this.

Role: Deployer

Classification: Minimal risk

Rationale: The system assesses machine conditions, not people, and falls into no area of Annex III. Nor is it a safety component of a product placed on the market; it is an in-house tool. This leaves the AI literacy obligation under Article 4. It would be different if the system intervened in the safety shutdown of an installation or the installation belonged to the critical supply of water, gas, heating or electricity — Annex III, point 2 would then be possible.

To do: Ensure AI literacy of the maintenance staff.; Lay down who approves maintenance orders, so that the prediction does not stop production unchecked.; Re-check the classification if the system intervenes in safety functions.; Monitor the prediction quality and do not trust it unchecked over time.

What matters: The large field of plant and process data mostly lies outside the AI Act, because it is not about people. Two boundaries should nevertheless be known: intervention in safety functions, and critical infrastructure under Annex III, point 2. For industrial companies this is an important relief — most projects in production and maintenance are free of the heavy obligations, which frees up effort for the few cases that really are about people.

Common mistake: The system is later extended with an evaluation of which maintenance teams fix faults fastest. It thereby evaluates employee performance and falls under Annex III, point 4.

title: Spelling and style aid for an authority's administrative decisions
text:
Use case: Spelling and style aid for an authority's administrative decisions

Scenario: An authority uses an AI-assisted writing aid. The case handler finishes writing the notice of decision, then the system smooths sentence structure and spelling and suggests more understandable wording. It changes nothing about content, reasoning or the decision; the case handler adopts or discards each suggestion.

Role: Deployer

Classification: Exemption under Article 6(3)

Rationale: The decision concerns benefits and thus an area that may be covered by Annex III, point 5(a). Here, however, the derogation under Article 6(3) applies: the system does not pose a significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights and does not materially influence the outcome of decision-making. Point (b) is met — it improves the result of a previously completed human activity. No profiling takes place. Under Article 6(4), the assessment must be documented.

To do: Record the assessment that the derogation applies in writing before putting the system into use.; Observe the registration obligation under Article 49(2) insofar as it falls on the provider, and provide the assessment to the authorities upon request.; Ensure through the work instructions that the system is only used after the draft is finished.; Ensure AI literacy of the case handlers.; Re-check the assessment if the system later makes suggestions on the substance of the text.

What matters: The derogation under Article 6(3) is not a free pass but a reasoned and documented decision. It requires two things at once: no significant risk and no material influence on the decision — and in addition one of the four cases in points (a) to (d). What matters here is the order in the procedure: the same tool would not be exempt if it helped formulate the decision instead of smoothing the finished one. Anyone wanting to use the derogation therefore designs the workflow so that it holds.

Common mistake: The authority relies on the derogation without documenting it. Article 6(4) requires documentation before putting the system into use — a justification added later during an inspection is too late.

title: Shift planning that ranks by reliability
text:
Use case: Shift planning that ranks by reliability

Scenario: A logistics centre plans its shifts with an AI system. Until recently, the system only worked with qualifications, working-time accounts and statutory rest periods. Now the company has extended it: it also takes into account how often someone has been absent at short notice in the past, and preferentially assigns the employees with the fewest absences to the well-paid night shifts.

Role: Deployer

Classification: High risk (Annex III)

Rationale: Annex III, point 4(b) covers the allocation of tasks based on individual behaviour or personal traits. Before the extension, the system only worked with fixed requirements and thus stayed outside this case; with absence behaviour as a criterion, planning becomes a behaviour-based allocation of tasks. Since the allocation also affects earning opportunities, it additionally touches on the terms of the work-related relationship.

To do: Before the extension, check whether the new calculation rule changes the classification — and record the result of this check.; Inform the workers' representatives and employees about the use.; Name a person who can overrule the system's shift assignments.; Check whether absence data may be used for this purpose at all; health data are specially protected.

What matters: A single new variable in the calculation can move a system into a different risk class without anything changing on the surface. The classification depends on the purpose and the criteria, not on the name of the tool. That is why every change to a system in use must come with the question whether it shifts the classification — and anyone who never asks the question does not notice the shift.

Common mistake: The extension is treated as a small improvement to a planning tool that has been harmless for years and therefore goes live without any new check.

title: Camera proctoring in a remote exam
text:
Use case: Camera proctoring in a remote exam

Scenario: A further-education institution lets candidates take final exams at home on their own computer. An AI system monitors the camera image and reports to the examination office if the gaze repeatedly moves away from the screen, a second person is in the picture or sounds suggest collusion. Reported cases are examined as attempted cheating.

Role: Deployer

Classification: High risk (Annex III)

Rationale: Annex III, point 3(d) lists AI systems intended to be used for monitoring and detecting prohibited behaviour of students during tests. The system does exactly that. The line to the prohibition is important: if the system inferred emotional states such as nervousness or stress from the camera image, it would be prohibited under Article 5(1)(f), because inferring emotions in education institutions is prohibited. Observing gaze direction and the presence of other persons stays short of that, but is close to this line.

To do: Exclude contractually and technically that the system evaluates emotions or emotional states.; Inform examinees before the exam about the use and the characteristics evaluated.; Have every report examined by a human before attempted cheating is assumed.; Consider a data protection impact assessment; observation inside the home is a serious intrusion.; Offer a fallback option for examinees for whom the technology does not work reliably.

What matters: With emotions, only a small step lies between high risk and prohibition. Evaluating the same camera image is permitted when it is about gaze direction and presence, and prohibited when emotions are inferred from it — in the workplace as in education institutions. Anyone buying such systems must have the evaluated characteristics named in detail, because the difference lies not in the product name but in the characteristics.

Common mistake: The provider advertises a detection of anomalies that tacitly includes signs of nervousness. With that, the use in education institutions slips into the prohibition without the institution noticing.

title: Automated performance evaluation in inside sales
text:
Use case: Automated performance evaluation in inside sales

Scenario: A wholesaler evaluates the telephone and quotation data of its inside sales team every month with an AI system. The system generates a score for each employee from call duration, closing rate and response times and sorts the employees into three groups. The grouping goes to the team leaders and is the basis for the annual reviews and variable pay.

Role: Deployer

Classification: High risk (Annex III)

Rationale: Annex III, point 4(b) lists AI systems for monitoring and evaluating the performance and behaviour of workers, as well as systems for making decisions affecting the terms of work-related relationships. Both apply, since the grouping feeds into variable pay. The derogation under Article 6(3) is ruled out because the system sorts the employees on the basis of personal traits and thereby performs profiling — where profiling takes place, a system from Annex III is always considered high-risk under the last sentence of Article 6(3).

To do: Entrust human oversight to a person who may change the grouping and does not merely pass it on.; Inform the workers' representatives and the evaluated employees before the start.; Tell the evaluated employees that a high-risk AI system takes part in the evaluation.; Check whether there is a legal basis for the continuous monitoring and whether an agreement with the works council is needed.; Give employees a way to object to the evaluation and to state their point of view.

What matters: Profiling is the bolt across the derogation. As soon as a system classifies, evaluates or predicts people on the basis of personal traits or their behaviour, it no longer helps to point to the derogation under Article 6(3) — the Regulation expressly excludes it in this case. Anyone who wants to check whether the derogation might apply therefore checks first: is a statement being formed here about individual people? If so, the check is over.

Common mistake: Businesses treat such scoring systems as a mere evaluation of data that already exists and overlook that condensing it into a score per person is itself the step that triggers the classification.

title: Learning-level assessment that determines the support track
text:
Use case: Learning-level assessment that determines the support track

Scenario: A school authority uses a learning platform that evaluates practice exercises. From these, an AI system estimates each pupil's level of performance in mathematics and recommends one of three support tracks. The school management assigns the pupils to the tracks on the basis of the recommendation.

Role: Deployer

Classification: High risk (Annex III)

Rationale: Annex III, point 3(c) lists AI systems intended to be used for assessing the appropriate level of education that an individual will receive or will be able to access. Assignment to support tracks is such an assessment. Point (b) is added, because the system evaluates learning outcomes and thereby steers the learning process. The derogation under Article 6(3) does not apply, because the system classifies individual pupils and the assignment follows the recommendation.

To do: As a public institution, carry out a fundamental rights impact assessment.; Inform parents and pupils that the system takes part in the assignment.; Enable teachers to deviate from the recommendation, and do not make this harder by requiring them to justify it.; Evaluate the recommendations to see whether certain groups regularly end up in the lower track.

What matters: A recommendation to a teacher and a turning point in someone's educational path are often the same thing. For minors, such a determination weighs particularly heavily, because it shapes the further path for a long time and can hardly be corrected. For your own cases, the question is helpful: how easily can the person concerned still reverse the result later? The harder it is, the less weight the argument carries that it is only a proposal.

Common mistake: The school considers the assessment a neutral measurement. But what is measured depends on the exercises and their weighting, and an assignment based on this measurement is a decision about the educational path.

title: Building a facial database from images on the internet
text:
Use case: Building a facial database from images on the internet

Scenario: A security services company wants to improve its access control. It downloads publicly accessible profile pictures from social networks en masse and uses an AI system to build a facial database from them, so that it can match visitors later. In addition, it feeds in footage from the surveillance cameras at its sites.

Role: Provider and Deployer

Classification: Prohibited practice

Rationale: Article 5(1)(e) prohibits the placing on the market, the putting into service for this specific purpose and the use of AI systems that create or expand facial recognition databases through the untargeted scraping of facial images from the internet or CCTV footage. Both sources are concerned here. That the images were publicly accessible is irrelevant — the prohibition attaches to untargeted scraping, not to accessibility.

To do: Stop building it and delete the database created in this way.; For access control, switch to methods in which the persons concerned knowingly allow themselves to be enrolled.; Bear in mind that biometric access control can still be high-risk under Annex III, point 1 even then.; Check under data protection law: facial images used for identification are biometric data of a specially protected category.

What matters: Publicly accessible does not mean freely usable. The prohibition is directed against untargeted collection — that is, against harvesting without connection to a specific purpose or a specific person. Anyone wanting to work biometrically must collect the data from the persons concerned themselves and for the specific purpose. And even then you are not done: permitted biometric systems are frequently high-risk under Annex III, point 1.

Common mistake: The company believes it is on the safe side by buying a ready-made data set. Besides creating, the prohibition also covers expanding and using such systems — and whoever buys, uses.

title: Job advertisements that the system targets
text:
