Use case: Job advertisements that the system targets

Scenario: A care service places its job advertisements through an advertising network. An AI system of the network decides which users are shown the advertisement, optimising for as many applications as possible per euro spent. The care service only sets budget and region and receives an evaluation of the impressions.

Role: Deployer

Classification: High risk (Annex III)

Rationale: Besides analysing applications, Annex III, point 4(a) expressly names placing targeted job advertisements. Anyone who has advertisements delivered through an optimising system uses an AI system for selection in this sense, because the pre-selection already decides who learns of the position at all. Who is provider and who is deployer in the individual case depends on how the advertising network makes the system available; the care service in any event uses it under its own authority.

To do: Ask the advertising network which characteristics the delivery is optimised for, and document the answer.; Check whether the delivery systematically excludes groups — for example by age or gender.; Examine the evaluation of the impressions for imbalances instead of only looking at the number of applications.; Name a person who oversees the use and can switch it off.

What matters: Selection begins before the first application. A system that only determines who sees an advertisement makes no decision about a person — and still falls under selection, because it shapes the pool of applicants. Anyone checking their own processes should therefore start at the beginning of the chain and not only where a decision is obviously made. Optimising for click success often leads to imbalances by itself, without anyone having intended them.

Common mistake: The company considers itself uninvolved because it only sets budget and region and the technology belongs to someone else. It nonetheless remains responsible for the use, and it must obtain information about the optimisation criteria from the provider rather than simply not having it.

title: Translation of technical manuals
text:
Use case: Translation of technical manuals

Scenario: A mechanical engineering company translates its operating manuals from German into English and Spanish with an AI system. The raw translations go to the technical writing team, which checks them for subject accuracy and approves them. Only then do they go to the customer with the machine.

Role: Deployer

Classification: Minimal risk

Rationale: The translation falls into no area of Annex III and touches no prohibited practice. The marking obligation for generated content under Article 50(2) does not apply here, because it does not apply to the extent that systems perform an assistive function for standard editing or do not substantially alter the input data provided or its semantics — a translation is meant precisely to preserve the meaning. This leaves the AI literacy obligation under Article 4. Product safety requirements for the correctness of the instructions continue to apply independently of this.

To do: Make the subject-matter review of the raw translation a binding step before any manual goes out.; Ensure AI literacy of the technical writing team.; Check safety-relevant passages particularly carefully; a mistranslated warning is a product problem.; Record who approved which version.

What matters: Article 50(2) contains an exception that covers many everyday tools: anyone who only edits in an assistive way or does not substantially alter the content need not mark it. Translating, summarising and linguistic smoothing generally fall under it; freely generating new content does not. The dividing line runs where editing existing content turns into inventing new content — and with your own tools this line is often crossed quickly.

Common mistake: In the next step, the same tool is used for advertising copy that it formulates freely. There the exception no longer holds, and the classification of the use must be reassessed.

title: Telematics tariff in motor insurance
text:
Use case: Telematics tariff in motor insurance

Scenario: An insurer offers a cheaper motor tariff for drivers who let an app run along. An AI system evaluates braking behaviour, acceleration and night driving and from this calculates a driving score that decides the discount for the following year.

Role: Provider and Deployer

Classification: Minimal risk

Rationale: Annex III, point 5(c) covers risk assessment and pricing in life and health insurance; motor insurance is not named there, and no other area of Annex III applies either. This leaves the AI literacy obligation under Article 4. Evaluating driving behaviour is nonetheless a sensitive processing under data protection law involving location data, and the discount can be an automated individual decision — that is a separate check outside the AI Act.

To do: Ensure AI literacy of the employees working with the system.; Clarify the legal basis under data protection law for the ongoing collection of driving data.; Re-check the classification if the driving score is used for other purposes.; Explain to customers in understandable terms which data are collected and how they affect the discount.

What matters: Not high-risk does not mean unregulated, and still less does it mean harmless. Here almost nothing of the AI Act applies, but a great deal of data protection law does. Anyone who takes the risk class as the only measure reaches the wrong result in exactly such cases — the classification only answers the question which obligations follow from the AI Act, not the question whether the project is acceptable.

Common mistake: Within the company, "does not fall under Annex III" turns into the message "uncritical, can go ahead as is". The check of the data processing is then skipped entirely, although here it is the real hurdle.

title: Model provider in the United States
text:
Use case: Model provider in the United States

Scenario: A medium-sized manufacturer has its technical enquiries answered by a language model that a provider based in the United States makes available through an application programming interface. In the process, customers' enquiries, including names, installation numbers and contact details, go to this provider's servers.

Role: Deployer

Classification: Minimal risk

Rationale: Answering technical enquiries falls into no area of Annex III; this leaves the AI literacy obligation under Article 4, and if customers talk directly with the system, the transparency obligation under Article 50(1) is added. Under data protection law, there is a transfer of personal data to a third country. It is permissible only on one of the bases provided for in data protection law — for example on the basis of an adequacy decision for the country of destination or of appropriate safeguards — and the current status of these bases must be checked before the decision.

To do: Determine the basis for the transfer to the third country and check its current status, instead of relying on an earlier assessment.; Conclude a data processing agreement with the provider.; Lay down which information is transmitted at all, and remove the rest beforehand.; Clarify and record in the contract whether the provider uses the inputs for its own training.; Inform customers that an AI system is answering and where their information goes.

What matters: With purchased models, the risk usually arises not from the classification but from the data path. Two questions decide almost every such case: what leaves the company, and what may the provider do with it? Both can be clarified contractually and technically, and the deployer must clarify both itself — the provider will not volunteer that it reuses inputs.

Common mistake: The transfer basis is checked once and then treated as permanently settled. The bases for third-country transfers have changed in the past; anyone who does not re-check will at some point be working without a valid basis.

title: Training an in-house model with customer data
text:
Use case: Training an in-house model with customer data

Scenario: A software house operates an accounting program for small businesses. It wants to use the booking texts entered by its customers to train its own AI system that will in future pre-assign accounts to bookings automatically. The booking texts contain names of suppliers, employees and private individuals.

Role: Provider

Classification: Minimal risk

Rationale: Pre-assigning accounts to bookings falls into no area of Annex III, so under the AI Act this leaves the AI literacy obligation under Article 4. The real hurdle lies in data protection law: the training is a new processing for a purpose other than performance of the contract and needs its own legal basis. It must also be clarified in which role the software house holds the customer data — if it processes them on behalf of its customers, it may not simply use them for its own purposes.

To do: Before training, clarify whether the data are processed on behalf of the customers; if so, use for own purposes without instructions is impermissible.; Determine a legal basis for the new purpose and assess the change of purpose.; Remove personal references from the training data insofar as they are not needed for the purpose.; Inform customers and data subjects about the processing.; Check whether the trained model can reproduce inputs, and counteract this.

What matters: Training data are the most frequently underestimated part of an AI project. The question is not only whether the data are available, but for what purpose they were collected and in which role you hold them. Anyone who processes data on behalf of their customers does not have them at their own disposal — and training projects fail on this more often than on the AI Act. This check belongs before the first training run, because a model trained with impermissible data can hardly be remedied afterwards.

Common mistake: The software house relies on a clause in its general terms and conditions that permits use for product improvement. Whether that holds as a basis for training on personal data is doubtful and must in any case be checked separately — all the more so if the data concern third parties who have nothing to do with the software house.

title: Pre-selection of applicants for a degree programme with restricted admission
text:
Use case: Pre-selection of applicants for a degree programme with restricted admission

Scenario: A university of applied sciences has more applicants than places for a degree programme. An AI system evaluates certificates, motivation letters and internship records and draws up a ranking. The selection committee invites the top 60 applicants to an interview.

Role: Deployer

Classification: High risk (Annex III)

Rationale: Annex III, point 3(a) lists AI systems intended to be used to determine access or admission or to assign natural persons to educational institutions. A ranking that determines who is invited takes part in admission. Since the system evaluates and classifies individual applicants on the basis of their documents, it performs profiling; the derogation under Article 6(3) is thus excluded under its last sentence.

To do: As a public institution, carry out a fundamental rights impact assessment before putting the system into use.; Inform applicants that the system takes part in admission.; Be able to disclose the ranking criteria and check them for unlawful discrimination.; Enable the selection committee to deviate from the ranking, and record such deviations.

What matters: A ranking appears more neutral than a decision, but it is one, because it draws the line. What counts for the classification is the effect in the procedure, not the form of the output. At the same time, the case shows that public institutions additionally owe the fundamental rights impact assessment for systems from Annex III — regardless of which area of the Annex is concerned.

Common mistake: The institution sees the ranking as a preparatory task under Article 6(3)(d). But the last sentence of that paragraph expressly excludes the derogation where profiling takes place, and an evaluation of individual applicants is profiling.

title: Purchased system offered under the company's own name
text:
Use case: Purchased system offered under the company's own name

Scenario: A recruitment services company buys a ready-made AI system for pre-selecting applicants from a software house. It puts its logo on the interface, names it after itself and makes it available to its client companies as its own product. Technically it changes nothing.

Role: Provider

Classification: High risk (Annex III)

Rationale: As applicant pre-selection, the system falls under Annex III, point 4(a) and is therefore high-risk. What matters here is the role: under Article 25(1)(a), anyone who puts their name or trademark on a high-risk AI system already placed on the market is considered a provider. The services company thereby becomes a provider and is subject to the full provider obligations under Article 16 — although it has not written a single line of program code. The original software house is then no longer the provider of this system, but must cooperate and provide documentation.

To do: Take on the provider obligations in full: risk management, data quality, technical documentation, record-keeping, accuracy and robustness.; Put a quality management system in place.; Carry out the conformity assessment procedure and register the system in the EU database.; Secure contractually from the software house the documentation and cooperation needed for these obligations.; Provide the client companies with instructions for use in accordance with Article 13.

What matters: Your own logo on someone else's high-risk system is the most expensive sticker in business. Article 25 knows three routes by which a deployer becomes a provider: putting on their own name, making a substantial modification, or changing the purpose in such a way that the system becomes high-risk. Anyone wanting to pass on someone else's system should know beforehand on which side of this line they will stand — afterwards the role is assigned and the obligations are there.

Common mistake: The contract with the software house lacks the obligation to hand over the technical documentation. The services company then owes it as provider, but cannot get hold of the documents.
